claims.text: A carefully trained machine-learning interatomic potential can capture phase free energies and fusion properties of multicomponent alloys with near-ab-initio fidelity.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to direct ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Active learning over representative solid and molten configurations can provide a training set suitable for fitting the proposed machine-learning potential.
Combining the fitted machine-learning potential with thermodynamic integration can accurately compute the free energy of each phase.
Training on ab initio solid and liquid data can represent the relevant vibrational and electron–vibration coupling modes.
The learned potential-energy surfaces will approximate first-principles forces with high fidelity.
High-fidelity approximation of first-principles forces enables less costly thermodynamic integration and free-energy calculations.
The proposed surrogate calculations will retain sufficient accuracy in vibrational and electronic interaction contributions.
For each tested alloy, the method will reproduce phase free energies within approximately 10 meV/atom of ab initio references.
For each tested alloy, the method will reproduce melting temperatures within approximately 50 K of ab initio references.
For each tested alloy, the method will reproduce enthalpies of fusion within approximately 10% of ab initio references.
The proposed applicability domain includes alloys with up to four principal components.
The proposed applicability domain extends from near-ambient temperature to 1.5 times the highest melting point of the alloy system.
The proposed pressure domain extends from ambient pressure to a few GPa.
Performance may degrade for alloy systems exhibiting complex phase transformations.
Performance may degrade when relevant electronic polarizations are insufficiently sampled in the training database.
Additional training data may restore robust coverage when complex transformations or electronic effects are under-sampled.
